content: Rapeseed, scientifically known as Brassica napus, is a bright yellow flowering plant belonging to the family Brassicaceae, which also includes mustard and cabbage. It is also referred to as rape, oilseed rape, rapa, rapaseed, and, in the case of a specific cultivar, canola. The name rapeseed originates from the Old English term for turnip, rapum. Some botanists classify the closely related Brassica campestris within the same species as B. napus. Rapeseed is cultivated for various purposes, including the production of animal feed, vegetable oil for human consumption, and biodiesel. Major producers include the European Union, Canada, the United States, Australia, China, and India. In India, rapeseed is grown on approximately 13% of the country's cropped land. According to the United States Department of Agriculture, rapeseed was the third-largest source of vegetable oil globally in 2000, following soybean and oil palm. It was also the second-largest source of protein meal, though its production was only one-fifth that of soybean meal. Global production of rapeseed has been increasing rapidly, with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) reporting 36 million tonnes produced in the 2003-2004 season and 46 million tonnes in 2004-2005. In Europe, rapeseed is primarily grown for animal feed due to its high lipid and moderate protein content. It is also a preferred crop for avoiding the importation of genetically modified (GMO) products. Natural rapeseed oil contains erucic acid, which is mildly toxic to humans in large doses but is used as a food additive in smaller amounts. The term canola (short for Canadian Oilseed, Low-Acid) was initially used by the Manitoba government to label low-erucic acid rapeseed during its experimental stages. Today, canola is a trade name for low-erucic acid rapeseed, though it is sometimes misapplied to other varieties. The rapeseed plant is the valuable, harvested component of the crop. It is also grown as a winter cover crop, providing soil coverage during winter and reducing nitrogen runoff. The plant can be plowed back into the soil or used as bedding. In some ecological or organic farming systems, livestock such as sheep or cattle are allowed to graze on the plants. Processing rapeseed for oil production yields rapeseed meal as a by-product, which is a high-protein animal feed competitive with soybean meal. This feed is primarily used for cattle but is also suitable for pigs and chickens, though it is less valuable for these animals. The meal has a very low content of glucosinolates, which are compounds that can disrupt metabolism in cattle and pigs. In China, rapeseed oil cake is also used as a fertilizer and for ornamental plants like bonsai. Additionally, rapeseed leaves and stems are edible, similar to bok choy or kale. Certain varieties of rapeseed, known as 油菜 (yóu cài, meaning oil vegetable in Chinese) or 菜の花 (nanohana in Japanese), are sold as greens, particularly in Asian grocery stores. Rapeseed is a significant nectar producer, and honeybees create a light-colored but peppery honey from it. This honey must be extracted immediately after processing, as it granulates quickly in the honeycomb, making extraction impossible. The honey is often blended with milder varieties or sold as bakery-grade honey. Rapeseed growers frequently contract with beekeepers to ensure the pollination of their crops. Canola oil, derived from rapeseed, contains both omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids in a 2:1 ratio. It is second only to flaxseed oil in omega-3 fatty acid content. Canola oil is considered one of the most heart-healthy oils, with reported benefits including reduced cholesterol levels, lower serum triglyceride levels, and prevention of platelet aggregation. In the UK, some farmers have begun producing cold-pressed rapeseed oil as a versatile cooking oil and dressing, similar to olive oil. Rapeseed oil is also used in the production of biodiesel for powering motor vehicles. Biodiesel made from rapeseed oil can be used in pure form in newer engines without causing damage and is often blended with standard diesel in varying ratios (e.g., 2% to 20% biodiesel). Historically, the costs of growing, crushing, and refining rapeseed biodiesel made it more expensive to produce than standard diesel fuel. However, the demand for rapeseed oil for biodiesel production has driven prices to very high levels. Rapeseed oil is the preferred oil stock for biodiesel production in much of Europe, partly because it yields more oil per unit of land area compared to other oil sources like soybeans. Rapeseed has been associated with adverse effects in individuals with asthma and hay fever. While some suggest that oilseed pollen is responsible for increased breathing difficulties, this is unlikely since rapeseed is an entomophilous crop, meaning its pollen is primarily transferred by insects. Others propose that inhalation of oilseed rape dust may be the cause, as allergies to the pollen itself are relatively rare. Another theory is that the distinctive and pungent smell of flowering rapeseed may lead hay fever sufferers to mistakenly attribute their symptoms to the plant. Alternatively, the sheer volume of rapeseed pollen in the air around farmland may trigger allergic reactions in hay fever sufferers, particularly after prolonged exposure to high levels. The Monsanto Company has genetically engineered new rapeseed cultivars resistant to its herbicide Roundup. Monsanto has aggressively pursued legal action against farmers found to have the Roundup Ready gene in their fields without paying a license fee. These farmers have claimed that the gene was blown into their fields and crossed with unaltered canola. Other farmers have reported that after spraying Roundup in non-canola fields to kill weeds before planting, Roundup Ready volunteers remain, causing additional expenses to remove these weeds. In a landmark legal case, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled in favor of Monsanto's patent infringement claim in the 2004 case Monsanto Canada Inc. v. Schmeiser. This case sparked international controversy as it was seen as legitimizing global patent protection for genetically modified crops. Rapeseed is susceptible to various pests and diseases. Common animal pests include harlequin bugs (Murgantia histrionica), flea beetles (Phyllotreta species), diamondback moths (Plutella xylostella), Bertha armyworms (Mamestra configurata), root maggots (Delia species), grasshoppers, lygus bugs (Lygus species), bronzed field beetle larvae, and snails and slugs. Diseases affecting rapeseed include beet western yellows virus, blackleg (caused by the fungus Leptosphaeria maculans), clubroot (caused by the protist Plasmodiophora brassicae), sclerotinia white stem rot, and white rust disease (Albugo candida). The genome of rapeseed is currently being sequenced by an international consortium, focusing on the 'A' genome component of the amphidiploid species Brassica napus.
